searchText: https://ledgerwatch.github.io/regenesis_plan.html this is what I managed to write so far about soft-fork hard-fork plan I am liking this more and more One question I am thinking about now is whether we want to change the CHAIN_ID after every ReGenesis event? It would mean that the transactions that did not make it into the chain before the event, will have to be explicitly recreated rather than failing on-chain due to lack of sufficient witnesses. I tend to say "yes" is the idea that this would happen in an automatic way in the consensus rules? is it worth considering the addition of a `regen` counter to isolate the tx domain without modding the current chain_id usage? no, I am now thinking that each ReGenesis event needs to be executed manually as a hard-fork, so we can justify our existence, and use it as an argument to get the difficulty bomb removed! 😉 lol. the state bloat bomb exactly. And that is how I got to the changing CHAIN_ID if someone wants to dissent, they can, and there is no replay attacks My immediate intuition is to get it right and have it happen automatically, but I'm just catching up on regenesis today <@!291925846556540928> I've been thinking that the first one is manual and we go into it planning for the second one to institute it on a regular cadence (but those are some really loose thoughts, I'm guessing there are problems hiding) and my most immediate concern while reading through is how this affects eth1+eth2 merger plans. thinking this is pretty opaque to the eth2 consensus layer as the merger is currently designed so that's good meaning, regenesis is a part of the entire unified consensus rules of the aggregate system but the clean separation of eth1/eth2 (user-layer/consensus) just means that the calls to eth1 from eth2 just require calling the correct regenesis'd version (this is all obvious, but just sanity checked it today) <@456226577798135808> what would you suggest target active state size is? and what regenesis time interval does that dictate? Target active state should be chosen so that you can get it fit in RAM on contemporary computers that is why I though to have events scheduled manually, because it is impossible for the chain to know that we can understand worst case bounds based on gas limit and block time yes, but chain does not know how much RAM is normally in the computers 🙂 > in RAM on contemporary computers so 6GB (8GB RAM with some room to spare?) > yes, but chain does not know how much RAM is normally in the computers 🙂 fair! but a regular cadence for 4 years then a slog of a political campaign for a 2x regenesis based on RAM advancements could also be a path... yes, I think both being too conservative and too aggressive is not good who has 6Gb on their computers these days? I thought it was more like 16 or 32 wife was just looking at lenovo Yoga yesterday which maxes at 8GB definitely depends on what type of consumer hardware we want to be able to run ethereum (or in the context of shards, a full-active-state single shard _in memory_) sometimes there's talk of being able to use the old laptop youhave laying around as a dedicated node in that case, you have to subtract ~4 years from the RAM race (I don't suggest my wife buys the Yoga. 8GB sounds terrible in the world of browser tabs) yes, that's fair i guess. doing ReGenesis too often has usability downsides, but we can try to find a good balance right would you say the state trie migration is a pre-req to regenesis? not necessarily, but we need to produce some data We still have the max block size with witnesses problem with regenesis, right? no, this is much easier to handle because most witnesses come with transactions, not blocks and the large ones can be knocked out in the tx pool but the blocks after regenesis maybe large and that is why we might need to do trie migration we need backtesting to see how quickly block size increase due to witnesses will fall after Regenesis event right, I see oh, and if we manage to do pre-consensus, then the large blocks won't matter so much, because everyone will know most of the block that will be mined, the only difference is the coinbase 🙂 I will include this into the doc as well pre-consensus? so instead of propagating large blocks over, we will be propagating miner's coinbases + headers https://ledgerwatch.github.io/regenesis_plan.html#Pre-consensus-network even without pre-consensus, if we simply make the block a sequence of tx IDs instead of listing all tx with all their witnesses (which by that time have already gotten everywhere), it should make large block problem easier this is sort of "thin block" optimisation known for ages 🙂 this is actually what will incentivise miners to follow pre-consensus rather than ignoring it because pre-consensus blocks can propagate faster _who_ is coming to pre-consensus on blocks? all the nodes. The miners can choose to obey or not is there sibel resistance here? well, this is what I am going to find out very soon. I am assuming that Avalanche is a good fit for such pre-consensus, but we will see avalanche at least requires a tokens in their consensus mechanism for baseline sibel resistance so in eth2, you could imagine leveraging the validator set in a sub-consensus but not exactly sure how that'd look here > It would mean that the transactions that did not make it into the chain before the eve Would likely break some contracts relying on chain_id aah just realized this channel exists copying my questions from the other channel One question about the regenesis model: how does it work between three epochs? That is, suppose you're currently in epoch N, and you're trying to access an account that was last modified during epoch N-2. Do you (i) need to provide both a witness for epoch N-2 and a witness for epoch N-1 to prove no subsequent change, or (ii) is there some crazy merge process when epoch N-1 ends that combines together the two states, or (iii) something else? Another question: are accounts that are in the inactive state (i) required to be part of an access list, or (ii) could tx execution unexpectedly trigger a requirement to access some particular account that has not been modifed in a long time? If the answers are (i) and (i), then this is remarkably similar to rent models from 1-2 years ago 😛 Except I guess with discrete epochs instead of continuous I believe the model doesn't care about historical epochs and only differentiates between active/inactive. Everything from **any** old epoch is inactive and the network only cares that transactions/blocks provide a proof for that data against any stateroot on or after the most recent epoch(regenesis) boundary. Similarity with state-rent is..... sneaky ... and I like it ... because it does state rent via the indirect mechanism of transaction fees. right, but I mean to prove inactive state from more than one epoch ago you either need multiple merkle proofs, or you need some kind of merge process I don't think so. At re-genesis boundary the state root stays the same, but everything gets moved to inactive state. I'm not following why multiple proofs would be needed (which I'm reasonably confident is not the case) okay, so suppose that: the state at the end of epoch 1 is S so at the beginning of epoch 2, the inactive state is S, and the active state is {} correct so far? then at the end of epoch 2, the active state becomes S' Now, suppose that, during epoch 3, you are trying to prove the state of some account that was last modified in epoch 1 let's say the account is x and the value is y you have to prove that (i) S[x] = y and (ii) x not in S' unless at the end of epoch 2 you somehow merge S and S' into a single tree which would be an O(N) operation I think this is where regenesis shines, because the network doesn't care about anything other than the active/inactive distinction. After a few epochs we would have a few snapshots and it becomes the transaction sender's problem of constructing a merkle proof against the most recent re-genesis state root. The network treats them as if they've been merged, the transaction producers are free to solve the problem however they choose. but there has to be some canonical way of representing the state roots..... I think the state root mechanism stays the same as it does today, but the client tracks only the active state, and any attempt to access inactive state terminates execution. aaah I see, there's no actual state root separation right ok, so the best metaphor then is not rent, it's partial-statelessness and there are zero consensus changes, it's all a higher-layer thing yeah, lots of good metaphors for us to use, purge, cleaning house, ... but it's not a "purge" per se in that the state isn't being purged from "the chain", it's being purged from what some clients store (I'm sure there will be clients that keep just storing the full state) right, it's being purged from the concern of the network It’s like RAM and hard drive? inactive state doesn't need the high speed access that active state does, so it makes a lot of sense to store them on different mediums. Ideally we end up seeing some sort of decentralized network that shards and distributes the inactive state or something like that.

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content:
One question about the regenesis model: how does it work between three epochs? That is, suppose you're currently in epoch N, and you're trying to access an account that was last modified during epoch N-2. Do you (i) need to provide both a witness for epoch N-2 and a witness for epoch N-1 to prove no subsequent change, or (ii) is there some crazy merge process when epoch N-1 ends that combines together the two states, or (iii) something else?
Another question: are accounts that are in the inactive state (i) required to be part of an access list, or (ii) could tx execution unexpectedly trigger a requirement to access some particular account that has not been modifed in a long time?
If the answers are (i) and (i), then this is remarkably similar to rent models from 1-2 years ago 😛
Except I guess with discrete epochs instead of continuous

excerpts.author: pipermerriam
excerpts.content: I believe the model doesn't care about historical epochs and only differentiates between active/inactive.  Everything from **any** old epoch is inactive and the network only cares that transactions/blocks provide a proof for that data against any stateroot on or after the most recent epoch(regenesis) boundary.

excerpts.author: pipermerriam
excerpts.content: Similarity with state-rent is..... sneaky ... and I like it ... because it does state rent via the indirect mechanism of transaction fees.

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: right, but I mean to prove inactive state from more than one epoch ago

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: you either need multiple merkle proofs, or you need some kind of merge process

excerpts.author: pipermerriam
excerpts.content: I don't think so.  At re-genesis boundary the state root stays the same, but everything gets moved to inactive state.  I'm not following why multiple proofs would be needed (which I'm reasonably confident is not the case)

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: okay, so suppose that:

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: the state at the end of epoch 1 is S

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: so at the beginning of epoch 2, the inactive state is S, and the active state is {}

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: correct so far?

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: then at the end of epoch 2, the active state becomes S'

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Now, suppose that, during epoch 3, you are trying to prove the state of some account that was last modified in epoch 1

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: let's say the account is x and the value is y

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: you have to prove that (i) S[x] = y and (ii) x not in S'

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: unless at the end of epoch 2 you somehow merge S and S'

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: into a single tree

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: which would be an O(N) operation

excerpts.author: pipermerriam
excerpts.content: I think this is where regenesis shines, because the network doesn't care about anything other than the active/inactive distinction.  After a few epochs we would have a few snapshots and it becomes the transaction sender's problem of constructing a merkle proof against the most recent re-genesis state root.  The network treats them as if they've been merged, the transaction producers are free to solve the problem however they choose.

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: but there has to be some canonical way of representing the state roots.....

excerpts.author: pipermerriam
